title: God loves all that he has made
source_text: Ἐπεὶ δὲ πεποίηκεν οὓς ἡγεῖται σκώληκας Χριστιανοὺς λέγοντας ὅτι τὴν οὐράνιον φορὰν ἀπολιπὼν ὁ θεὸς καὶ τὴν τοσαύτην γῆν παριδὼν ἡμῖν μόνοις πολιτεύεται καὶ πρὸς ἡμᾶς ἐπικηρυκεύεται καὶ πέμπων οὐ διαλείπει καὶ ζητῶν. ὅπως ἀεὶ συνῶμεν αὐτῷ, λεκτέον ὅτι τὰ μὴ λεγόμενα πρὸς ἡμῶν περιτίθησιν ἡμῖν, τοῖς καὶ ἀναγινώσκουσι καὶ γινώσκουσιν ὅτι ἀγαπᾷ πάντα τὰ ὄντα ὁ θεὸς καὶ οὐδὲν βδελύσσεται ὧν ἐποίησεν· οὐδὲ γὰρ ἂν μισῶν τι κατεσκεύασεν. ἀνέγνωμεν δὲ καὶ τό· „φείδῃ δὲ πάντων, ὅτι σά ἐστι πάντα. φιλόψυχε. τὸ γὰρ ἄφθαρτόν (σου) πνεῦμά ἐστιν ἐν πᾶσι· διὸ καὶ τοὺς παραπίπτοντας κατ᾿ ὀλίγον ἐλέγχεις. καὶ ἐν οἷς ἁμαρτάνουσιν ὑπομιμνήσκων νουθετεῖς.“ πῶς δὲ δυνάμεθα λέγειν τὴν οὐράνιον φορὰν καὶ τὸν πάντα κόσμον ἀπολιπόντα τὸν θεὸν καὶ τὴν τοσαύτην γῆν παριδόντα ἡμῖν μόνοις ἐμπολιτεύεσθαι; οἵτινες ἐν ταῖς εὐχαῖς εὕρομεν δεῖν τι λέγειν φρονοῦντας ὅτι „τοῦ ἐλέους κυρίου πλήρης ἡ γῆ,“ καὶ „ἔλεος κυρίου ἐπὶ πᾶσαν σάρκα,“ καὶ ὅτι ἀγαθὸς ὢν ὁ θεὸς „ἀνατέλλει“ „τὸν ἥλιον αὐτοῦ ἐπὶ πονηροὺς καὶ ἀγαθοὺς καὶ βρέχει ἐπὶ δικαίους καὶ ἀδίκους,“ καὶ ἡμᾶς, ἵνα γενώμεθα αὐτοῦ υἱοὶ, ἐπὶ τὰ παραπλήσια προτρέπων καὶ διδάσκων εἰς πάντας ἡμᾶς ἀνθρώπους κατὰ τὸ δυνατὸν ἐκτείνειν τὰς εὐποιΐας, καὶ γὰρ αὐτὸς εἴρηται „σωτὴρ πάντων ἀνθρώπων, μάλιστα πιστῶν,“ καὶ ὁ Χριστὸς αὐτοῦ „ἱλασμὸς“ εἶναι „περὶ τῶν ἁμαρτιῶν ἡμῶν, οὐ περὶ τῶν ἡμετέρων δὲ μόνων ἀλλὰ καὶ περὶ ὅλου τοῦ κόσμου,“ καὶ τάχα μὲν οὐ ταῦτα. ὅσα ἀνέγραψεν ὁ Κέλσος, ἄλλα δέ τινα ἰδιωτικὰ εἴποιεν ἂν Ἰουδαίων τινὲς, ἀλλ᾿ οὔτι γε καὶ Χριστιανοὶ, οἱ διδαχθέντες ὅτι „συνίστησι τὴν ἑαυτοῦ ἀγάπην εἰς ἡμᾶς ὁ θεὸς, ὅτι ἔτι ἁμαρτωλῶν ὄντων ἡμῶν Χριστὸς ὑπὲρ ἡμῶν ἀπέθανε.“ καίτοι γε „μόγις τις ὑπὲρ τοῦ δικαίου ἀποθανεῖται· ὑπὲρ γὰρ τοῦ ἀγαθοῦ τάχα τις καὶ τολμᾷ ἀποθανεῖν.“ νυνὶ δὲ ὑπὲρ τῶν πανταχοῦ ἁμαρτωλῶν. ἵνα καταλίπωσι τὴν ἁμαρτίαν καὶ πιστεύσωσι τῷ θεῷ ἑαυτοὺς, ἐπιδεδημηκέναι κεκήρυκται ὁ Ἰησοῦς, πατρίῳ τινὶ τοῖς λόγοις τούτοις συνηθείᾳ καὶ Χριστὸς εἶναι λεγόμενος τοῦ θεοῦ.
pass_a_gloss: Since he has made (ποιέω, represented) those he considers (ἡγέομαι) worms, Christians, saying that God, having left (ἀπολείπω) the heavenly revolution (οὐράνιος φορά) and having overlooked (παροράω) the so great earth, lives as citizen (πολιτεύομαι) for us alone, and treats by herald (ἐπικηρυκεύομαι) with us, and sending does not leave off (διαλείπω), and seeking how we may always be with (σύνειμι) him, it must be said (λεκτέον) that he puts around (περιτίθημι, attributes) to us things not said by us, who both read (ἀναγινώσκω) and know (γινώσκω) that God loves (ἀγαπάω) all beings and loathes (βδελύσσομαι) nothing of what he made; for he would not have constructed (κατασκευάζω) anything hating (μισέω) it. And we have read also this: ‘You spare (φείδομαι) all, because all are yours, lover of souls (φιλόψυχος). For your incorruptible (ἄφθαρτος) Spirit (πνεῦμα) is in all; therefore also those falling aside (παραπίπτω) little by little (κατ’ ὀλίγον) you convict/correct (ἐλέγχω), and reminding (ὑπομιμνῄσκω) [them] in what they sin you admonish (νουθετέω).’ How can we say that God, having left the heavenly revolution and the whole world and having overlooked the so great earth, lives as citizen (ἐμπολιτεύομαι) among us alone? we who have found (εὑρίσκω) that in the prayers we must (δεῖ) say something thinking (φρονέω) that ‘of the mercy (ἔλεος) of the Lord full is the earth’, and ‘mercy of the Lord upon all flesh (σάρξ)’, and that God, being good (ἀγαθός), ‘makes rise (ἀνατέλλω) his sun upon evil and good, and rains (βρέχω) upon just and unjust’, and urging (προτρέπω) us, so that we may become his sons (υἱός), to the like, and teaching [us] to extend (ἐκτείνω) good deeds (εὐποιΐα) to all men according to what is possible (κατὰ τὸ δυνατόν); for he himself is said [to be] ‘saviour (σωτήρ) of all men, especially of believers (πιστός)’, and his Christ to be ‘propitiation (ἱλασμός) for our sins, not for ours only but also for the whole world’. And perhaps not these things which Celsus recorded (ἀναγράφω), but some other unlearned/naive (ἰδιωτικός) things some of the Jews might say, but certainly not Christians, who were taught that ‘God commends (συνίστημι) his own love (ἀγάπη) toward us, that while we were still sinners (ἁμαρτωλός) Christ died for us’. And yet ‘scarcely (μόγις) will someone die for the righteous (δίκαιος); for for the good (ἀγαθός) perhaps someone even dares (τολμάω) to die’. But now (νυνί) for sinners everywhere (πανταχοῦ), so that they may leave (καταλείπω) sin and entrust (πιστεύω) themselves to God, Jesus has been proclaimed (κηρύσσω) to have come to dwell (ἐπιδημέω), by a certain ancestral (πάτριος) usage (συνήθεια) in these words/writings (λόγοι) being called also Christ of God.
pass_b_english: Celsus has represented those he considers worms, the Christians, as saying that “God has left the motion of the heavens and disregarded the vast earth, and makes his home among us alone, sends his envoys to us, and never ceases sending and seeking how we may be with him forever.” To this we must reply that he attributes to us things that we do not say. For we read and know that God loves all things that exist and loathes none of the things he has made, for he would not have fashioned anything if he hated it (Wisdom of Solomon 11:24). We have also read: “You spare all things, for they are yours, O Lover of souls. For your imperishable Spirit is in all things. Therefore you correct little by little those who fall away, and you admonish them by reminding them of the things in which they sin” (Wisdom of Solomon 11:26–12:2).

How could we say that God has left the motion of the heavens and the whole world, and disregarded the vast earth, to make his home among us alone? We have found that in our prayers we must speak as people convinced that “the earth is full of the mercy of the Lord” (Psalm 33:5), and that “the mercy of the Lord is upon all flesh” (Sirach 18:13); and that God, being good, “makes his sun rise on the evil and on the good, and sends rain on the just and on the unjust” (Matthew 5:45). He urges us to do the like, so that we may become his sons (Matthew 5:44–45), and teaches us to extend our good deeds to all people as far as we can. For he himself is called “the Saviour of all people, especially of believers” (1 Timothy 4:10), and his Christ is called “the propitiation for our sins, and not for ours only but also for the whole world” (1 John 2:2).

Perhaps some of the Jews might say, not the things Celsus has recorded, but certain other naive things; but certainly not Christians, who have been taught that “God shows his own love for us in that, while we were still sinners, Christ died for us” (Romans 5:8). And yet “one will scarcely die for a righteous man; though for a good man someone might perhaps even dare to die” (Romans 5:7). But as it is, Jesus is proclaimed to have come for sinners everywhere, so that they may leave sin behind and entrust themselves to God; and by a usage long established in these writings he is also called the Christ of God.

choices.term: πατρίῳ τινὶ τοῖς λόγοις τούτοις συνηθείᾳ
choices.choice: πατρίῳ τινὶ τοῖς λόγοις τούτοις συνηθείᾳ: 'a usage native to these Scriptures' -> 'a usage long established in these writings' (λόγοι is not 'Scriptures' outright; 'native' was loose for πάτριος)

Checked: Celsus's words in double quotation marks; Wisdom 11:24 kept unquoted (indirect in Greek); Wisdom 11:26–12:2, LXX Psalm 32:5 = Psalm 33:5, Sirach 18:13, Matthew 5:45, 1 Timothy 4:10, 1 John 2:2, Romans 5:8 and 5:7 all verified

Celsus’s words in the opening sentence are Origen’s re-quotation of 4.23, here without ‘the whole world’ and without μόνους after πρὸς ἡμᾶς; translated as they stand in this chapter. πολιτεύεται / ἐμπολιτεύεσθαι (live as a citizen, have one’s commonwealth) rendered ‘makes his home among’; ἐπικηρυκεύεται (treat through heralds) rendered ‘sends his envoys’. Wisdom of Solomon 11:24 is given in indirect, third-person form in Greek (ὅτι ἀγαπᾷ … ὁ θεός), so it is not put in quotation marks; 11:26–12:2 is quoted directly; σου in 12:1 is an editorial supplement in Koetschau, followed; φιλόψυχε rendered ‘O Lover of souls’ (LXX has δέσποτα φιλόψυχε). LXX Psalm 32:5 = English Psalm 33:5 (wording matches; compare LXX 118:64 = English 119:64, ‘your mercy, Lord’). Sirach 18:13 (ἔλεος δὲ κυρίου ἐπὶ πᾶσαν σάρκα). 1 John 2:2 ἱλασμός rendered ‘propitiation’. Romans 5:8 is cited before 5:7, in Origen’s order; Origen reads μόγις for NT μόλις. ἰδιωτικά rendered ‘naive’ (lay, unlearned); it could also mean ‘peculiar to themselves’. ‘These writings’ renders τοῖς λόγοις τούτοις, taken as the scriptural words just cited; πατρίῳ συνηθείᾳ rendered ‘a usage long established’; ‘the Christ of God’ matches Luke 9:20 but is used here as a title, not a quotation, so uncited. ‘Come for sinners’ may echo 1 Timothy 1:15; uncited.
